title: Text
description: One prayer, blessing or poem with its word-by-word breakdown. Stored in processed/json/<id>.json.

id.description: Matches the file name, which is the input file's name: menucha_vsimcha for texts/menucha_vsimcha.txt.

title.description: The text's commonly used name, transliterated, e.g. "Menucha V'simcha". For part of a prayer: "Prayer: Part", e.g. "Havdala: Hinei El".

kind.description: poem: lines of verse. prose: continuous text.

sections.description: Natural divisions of the text: stanzas of a poem, paragraphs or blessings of prose. A text with no divisions has one section.

section.description: A refrain or other repeated stanza appears only once, where it first occurs; later repetitions are left out. It counts as a repetition only if its words are identical to the first occurrence (ignoring punctuation); if any word differs, it is a new section.

title.description: Name of the section, e.g. "Avot" or "V'ahavta". Given when the section has a commonly used name; left out otherwise, e.g. for the stanzas of a poem.

line.description: The smallest natural unit of the text: a verse of a poem, a pasuk, or a sentence of text that isn't a pasuk. A response added after a pasuk, such as כֵּן תִּהְיֶה לָּנוּ, is its own line.

hebrew.description: The full line, with nikud, keeping its punctuation, such as the sof pasuk ׃. When the source has no punctuation, a verse from the Tanakh ends with ׃ and has a comma between its clauses, and nowhere else.

clauses.description: The line divided into its clauses, in order. Together they cover the whole line: only punctuation and spaces are left between them.

clause.description: A subsentence of the line, shown on the Anki cards of its words instead of the whole line: a clause with its verb (or, without a verb, what it says about its subject) and everything attached to it, usually ending at a comma. A long clause is split at its main pause, as the cantillation divides it, and a list of short parallel parts joined by ו stays together. A line that is one clause has a single clause. Clauses don't overlap: a relative clause inside another clause splits it into three, וְהָיוּ הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה, אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוְּךָ הַיּוֹם, עַל־לְבָבֶךָ.

hebrew.description: Copied from the line as it stands, without punctuation at either end: כִּי עָזִּי וְזִמְרָת יָהּ יְיָ, בְּכָל־לְבָבְךָ וּבְכָל־נַפְשְׁךָ וּבְכָל־מְאֹדֶךָ.

translation.description: The part of the line's translation that translates this clause, following the same rules (words with no Hebrew counterpart in [square brackets]); a clause that is the whole line has the line's translation.

words.description: Words joined by a maqaf are separate words, each with its own root; the maqaf stays on the first: בְּכָל־לְבָבְךָ is בְּכָל־ (with all of) and לְבָבְךָ (your heart). Words joined by a maqaf are always in the same clause.

hebrew.description: The word as it appears in the line, without punctuation; a maqaf stays: מְאֹדֶךָ without the ׃ that ends its verse, בְּכָל־ with its maqaf.

meaning.description: Meaning of the word in this context, following the traditional translation of the line.

literal.description: The literal meaning, given only where the meaning departs from it: a verb whose traditional translation uses another tense than its form, or an idiom. Outputs show it after the meaning, as in: and she gives (lit. and she gave). E.g. וַתִּתֵּן (and she gives) has the literal meaning "and she gave", בְּחֵפֶץ (willingly) has "with desire".

parts.description: Prefixes, base word and suffixes, in order, each with its meaning in context. A single entry if the word is not split. Keep the ל of an infinitive with its verb: לְאַמֵּץ (to strengthen) is one infinitive-construct part. A preposition with a merged article is one preposition part with "the" in its meaning: לַ־ (for the). A plural noun with a pronoun suffix splits into its construct plural and the full plural suffix. The shared letters (if present) appear in both: אֱלֹהֵינוּ (our God) is אֱלֹהֵי (God of) and ־ֵינוּ (our).

root.description: Key into processed/json/roots.json. The root of the word, whenever it has one. Left out only when the root is neither commonly taught nor shared with any other word, biblical or modern Hebrew, names included: רְאֵמִים (wild oxen) has no root, since no other word shares ר-א-ם. A root is kept even when its other words have an unrelated meaning; the root's meaning then lists both, e.g. "bread; to fight". Names follow the same rule. Function words such as prepositions, adverbs and particles follow the same test: עַל (upon) has the root ע-ל-ה, shared with עֲלִיָּה (going up). Words with no root, such as pronouns, כִּי and לֹא, have none.

part.description: One component of a word. Store every grammatical fact the Hebrew marks; outputs decide which ones to print and how to label them.

hebrew.description: Prefixes end with a maqaf and suffixes start with one: וְ־ (and), ־ָיו (his). A base word is written as it stands on its own, undoing changes caused by its prefixes and suffixes (dagesh, vowels, endings); a noun or verb that takes a suffix keeps its construct form. E.g. יְהוּדִים in לַיְּהוּדִים, כָּל־ in וּבְכָל־, שֶׁבֶת in בְּשִׁבְתְּךָ, אֶל־ in אֵלָיו.

meaning.description: The literal meaning, following the part's grammatical form, even where the word's meaning follows a traditional translation: תִּתֵּן in וַתִּתֵּן is "she will give", its written future, although the word's meaning is "and she gives". A part in construct ends in "of": יוֹם (day of), מַלְכוּת (kingdom of) in מַלְכוּתוֹ.

pos.description: Particles are words that fit no other part of speech, such as the relative אֲשֶׁר (that), the object marker אֵת, הִנֵּה (behold) and סֶלָה (Selah); the object marker's meaning is "(marks the direct object)".

type.description: Kind of pronoun; only on pos pronoun. Pronoun suffixes are always personal.

form.description: After a vav that flips the tense (vav consecutive), the vav part is marked consecutive, and the verb part keeps its written form, past or future, with the meaning of that form: וַתִּתֵּן is וַ־ (and, consecutive) and תִּתֵּן (she will give, future); וּשְׁאַבְתֶּם is וּ־ (and, consecutive) and שְׁאַבְתֶּם (you drew, past). The word's meaning shows the flipped tense: וַיְהִי (and He became), וּשְׁאַבְתֶּם (and you shall draw). When the traditional translation uses another tense, such as the present in a timeless description, the word's meaning follows the translation and its literal gives the flipped tense: וַתִּתֵּן (and she gives), with the literal meaning "and she gave". Present and participle are the same Hebrew form (beinoni); choose by how the word functions. present: the verb of its clause, e.g. מְעִידִים (they testify). participle: works as a noun or adjective (takes the article הַ, is in construct, describes a noun, or means "one who…"), e.g. גּוֹאֵל (redeemer), מִתְעַנְּגִים in הַמִּתְעַנְּגִים (who delight). passive-participle: every passive form (the קָטוּל pattern, Pu'al/Hof'al מְ־/מֻ־ forms) whatever its function, e.g. בְּרוּאִים (created).

construct.description: True if the word is in construct (smichut) form. Also true for a noun or participle with a pronoun suffix, since the suffix attaches to the construct form.

pattern.description: The template from grammar/nouns.md the noun is built with, when it has one; only on nouns. mem-prefix: a מ that isn't a root letter, e.g. מִצְוָה (commandment), מָרוֹם (height). tav-prefix: a ת that isn't a root letter, e.g. תְּפִלָּה (prayer). vav-tav-ending: a וּת ending that isn't a root letter, e.g. מַלְכוּת (kingdom). A noun with a מ or ת prefix takes that pattern even if it also has an ending, e.g. מְנוּחָה (rest) is mem-prefix. Left out for nouns that are only a root with vowels, such as דֶּרֶךְ or קִדּוּשׁ, or have only a plain feminine ending, such as שִׂמְחָה or יְשׁוּעָה: a pattern is marked only by added letters, never by vowels alone (see meta/conventions.md).

consecutive.description: True for a vav that flips the tense of the verb after it (vav consecutive): וַ־ in וַתִּתֵּן, וְ־ in וְאָהַבְתָּ. Only on conjunctions.

language.description: Language of the part when it isn't Hebrew; left out for Hebrew. Mark a part only when its form belongs to the other language: prefixes shared by Hebrew and Aramaic (וְ־, בְּ־, לְ־) follow the language of the surrounding text. E.g. רַבָּה (great), דְּ־ (of) and the ending ־ָא (the) are Aramaic.

allOf.description: Only verbs have binyan and form; verbs must have both.
Only pronouns have a type; pronouns must have one.
Personal pronouns and pronoun suffixes have person and number (gender is required except in 1st person, see below).
2nd and 3rd person personal pronouns and pronoun suffixes have gender.
Demonstratives have gender and number but no person ("common" gender for אֵלֶּה).
Interrogatives have no person, gender or number.
Nouns and adjectives always have gender and number.
Past and future verbs have person and number (gender is required except in 1st person, see below).
2nd and 3rd person past and future verbs have gender.
Imperatives are 2nd person with gender and number.
Present tense and participles have gender and number but no person.
Infinitives have no person, gender or number.
1st person has no gender in Hebrew.

root.description: 3 or 4 Hebrew letters separated by hyphens, e.g. "ש-מ-ר". Only the last letter may be a final form, and it must be one where it exists ("ל-א-ך", not "ל-א-כ"), so each root has exactly one spelling.
